Degenerative myelopathy

A retrospective canine study reported longer time to loss of ambulation or euthanasia in the higher-output protocol group than in the lower-output and historical comparison groups. These outcomes are vulnerable to selection, treatment, and historical-control bias, so the finding does not establish that PBM slowed disease progression.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A retrospective canine study reported longer time to loss of ambulation or euthanasia in the higher-output protocol group than in the lower-output and historical comparison groups. These outcomes are vulnerable to selection, treatment, and historical-control bias, so the finding does not establish that PBM slowed disease progression.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact database category contains one unique publication, not a series of independent studies. Miller et al. retrospectively compared two treatment protocols in 20 dogs receiving rehabilitation. The groups differed in wavelength and output, and the study used published historical data as a benchmark rather than a concurrent control. (Miller et al. 2020)

Human and clinical evidence

No human clinical evidence was identified in this category. The single report is a veterinary clinical cohort, not a human trial; it provides no independent replication or estimate of efficacy in people.

Animal evidence

The cohort comprised 20 dogs with degenerative myelopathy: six received protocol A and 14 received protocol B. The authors reported longer time to loss of ambulation or euthanasia in protocol B than in protocol A and historical data. Rehabilitation was co-administered, and the retrospective comparison cannot separate treatment effects from baseline differences, care choices, or historical changes.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No in-vitro or ex-vivo study appears in the exact category. Mechanistic work, if available in broader PBM research, cannot be treated as clinical confirmation for canine degenerative myelopathy.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The database records 904 nm near-infrared light at 0.5 W for protocol A and 980 nm near-infrared light at 6–12 W for protocol B, both alongside rehabilitation. These widely different exposures do not establish an optimal wavelength or dose. The publication does not provide a randomized comparison capable of validating either protocol.

Interpretation

This is hypothesis-generating veterinary evidence only. Historical controls, small and unequal protocol groups, rehabilitation co-treatment, and retrospective allocation limit causal interpretation. Replication should use prospective randomized canine cohorts, matched rehabilitation, blinded functional assessment, and prespecified survival and quality-of-life outcomes. Human studies would be needed before drawing conclusions for people.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for survival benefit. One retrospective comparison used different PBM protocols and historical controls.
Publications and records1 unique title in Nervous system > Degenerative Myelopathy.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

This indication has one database publication: a retrospective comparison of 20 dogs receiving rehabilitation plus one of two PBM protocols. The protocol groups differed substantially in wavelength and output, and the comparison used published historical data rather than a concurrent control. Further prospective work should standardize rehabilitation and assess survival and quality of life.
